ety.text: From Middle English nose, from Old English nosu, from Proto-West Germanic *nosu, variant of *nasō, old dual from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s- ~ *nh₂es- (“nose, nostril”). See also Saterland Frisian Noose, West Frisian noas, Dutch neus, Swedish nos, Norwegian nos (“snout”), Low German Nääs, German Nase, Swedish näsa, Norwegian nese, Danish næse (“nose”); also Latin nāris (“nostril”), nāsus (“nose”), Lithuanian nósis, Russian нос (nos), Sanskrit नासा (nā́sā, “nostrils”).

senses.d: A protuberance on the face housing the nostrils, which are used to breathe or smell.
ex: She had a small nose between two sparkling blue eyes.

senses.d: A snout, the nose of an animal.
The tip of an object.
ex: the nose of a tea-kettle, a bellows, or a fighter plane

senses.d: The bulge on the side of a piece of a jigsaw puzzle, that fits into the hole of its adjacent piece.
The length of a horse’s nose, used to indicate the distance between horses at the finish of a race, or any very close race.
ex: Red Rum only won by a nose.

senses.d: A perfumer.
The sense of smell.
ex: We are not offended with […] a dog for a better nose than his master.

senses.d: Bouquet, the smell of something, especially wine.
The skill in recognising bouquet.
ex: It is essential that a winetaster develops a good nose.

senses.d: Skill at finding information.
ex: A successful tabloid reporter has a nose for gossip.

senses.d: To move cautiously by advancing its front end.
ex: The ship nosed through the minefield.

senses.d: To snoop.
ex: She was nosing around other people’s business.

senses.d: To detect by smell or as if by smell.
ex: […] if you finde him not this moneth, you ſhall noſe him as you go vp the ſtaires into the Lobby.
Dogs hurried out to nose Edmund[.]

senses.d: To push with one's nose; to nuzzle.
ex: [L]ambs are glad / Nosing the mother's udder, and the bird / Makes his heart voice among the blaze of flowers: […]

senses.d: To defeat (as in a race or other contest) by a narrow margin; sometimes with out.
To utter in a nasal manner; to pronounce with a nasal twang.
ex: It makes far better musick when you nose Sternold's, or Wisdom's meeter.

senses.d: To furnish with a nose.
To confront; be closely face to face or opposite to.
To dive down in a steep angle; to nosedive
To travel with the nose of the plane/ship aimed in a particular direction.
ex: We have to get it nosing down.

From Middle French trompe, from Old French trompe, from Frankish *trumpa, *trumba (“trumpet”), ultimately from an imitative Germanic word akin to Old Dutch drumba, trumba (“trumpet, horn”), Old High German trumba, trumpa, Old Norse trumba. Doublet of trombe.

New Latin nostalgiabor. English nostalgia From New Latin nostalgia, coined by Johannes Hofer in 1688 from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “returning home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”), calquing German Heimweh. Ancient Greek *νοσταλγία (*nostalgía) is unattested. Transferred sense probably influenced by French nostalgie, especially in literature. Compare Italian nostalgia, Spanish nostalgia, Portuguese nostalgia and French nostalgie.

senses.d: A longing for home or familiar surroundings; homesickness.
ex: Seeing food at camp similar to his mother's cooking sent a wave of nostalgia through him.

senses.d: A bittersweet yearning for the things of the past.
ex: an alumnus' feelings of nostalgia for his/her years in high school

ety.text: First attested in the 16th century. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese soydade, from Latin sōlitātem (“solitude”). The word’s irregular phonetic development is likely due to analogy with words such as saudar (“to wish good health”) and saudade (“salvation”, from Latin *salūtātem).
